linguisticReconstructions.claim: The jamu is a patrilineal clan name: it denotes membership in a descent group, not individual filiation to a father.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: The jamuw dictionary gives the entry Fófana two statuses, hɔ̀rɔn — the free, non-artisanal condition in the sense Charry defines the term — and wage, which it does not gloss. Neither is a nyamakala caste: the jamu orders a condition, not a hereditary trade.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Dioula, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the Dioula people's fiche.

sources.title: Beyond the Mali Empire — A New Paradigm for the Sunjata Epic
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Universiteit Leiden. Critical work on the transmission of the epic and on the jamu as a social institution rather than as historical memory; used here for the nature of the jamu, not to date an ancestor.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Onomastic annex of the Bamadaba, an electronic Bambara-French dictionary supplementing the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA); the clan-name annex is identified as such by Vydrin, "Vers une lexicographie mandingue sur la base de grands corpus annotés," Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. 375 entries in MDF format, consulted from the complete file. The file provides no legend for its markers, and the reading adopted here is the one the file imposes: \ca carries the Mandingo status terms themselves (nùmu, jèli, hɔ́rɔn, garanke, finɛ, tontigi, wage, gesere); \sn is read as senankun because the Kúyate entry annotates its own \sn Keyita line with a caveat stating that this particular relation is a friendly understanding and not a senankuya. \sn links are not systematically reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is therefore cited according to the entry that carries it, named in the claim or the gap.

sources.title: A Guide to the Jembe
sources.notes: Charry, Eric, Percussive Notes 34(2), April 1996, pp. 66-72; the author is the ethnomusicologist of Mande Music (University of Chicago Press, 2000). Article in a specialist trade journal, not a peer-reviewed journal: it is cited here for the attribution of jamuw to Mandingo social statuses (numu, jeli, horon), which it states by name clan by clan, and not for the history of the jembe.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. She sets out what the pact requires: the relation holds in perpetuity for the entire descent of both lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — variably applied today, she notes — and mutual assistance is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair covered by this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside it.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 onward. Cited for the caveat it carries: the idea that joking kinship would ease conflict is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed rather than as a measured effect. The starting page is verified, the ending page is not.

gaps.reason: No bearer has been attached to the jamu Fofana by the sources consulted: neither the Histoire générale de l'Afrique, which nonetheless names clan by clan the lineages that rallied to Soundiata, nor the jamuw dictionary, nor Charry attaches it to a person.

Fofana is borne in both the Mandingo and Soninke areas without a dedicated source establishing two distinct origins. The jamuw dictionary treats this dispersion under a single entry — it attaches five dialect-area codes to it without developing them — and lists Fònba, Magasa, Dancogo, Kamara and Diomandé among its equivalences, clan names of other peoples held to be the same. An equivalence is not a homonymy: it states that two names denote the same group, not that the same name denotes two.
